analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have added dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare for its roughly 60 million beneficiaries, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added dental, vision, and hearing care to Medicare, which today does not cover them. Seniors would get coverage for cleanings, fillings, dentures, eye exams and glasses, hearing exams and hearing aids, phased in over several years with caps on what Medicare pays. The bill was introduced by Rep. Lloyd Doggett with 114 Democratic cosponsors but no Republican support, was sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — mostly seniors and people with disabilities — who today pay out of pocket or go without dental care, glasses, and hearing aids. The bill gave fuller, faster coverage to low-income beneficiaries. Dentists, optometrists, audiologists, and hearing-aid makers would also gain a large new stream of Medicare patients and payments.

how_it_helps.text: Adds coverage of cleanings, exams, fillings, root canals, crowns, dentures, and emergency dental care to Medicare, phased in to 80% federal payment by 2025 [S2, S3].
Adds annual routine eye exams plus coverage of eyeglasses, contact lenses, and low-vision devices, with inflation-adjusted dollar caps [S2, S3].
Adds routine hearing exams and hearing aids, covered at 80% with one hearing aid per ear every four years [S2, S3].
Gives low-income beneficiaries fuller coverage sooner — 80% payment for basic dental services starting in 2023 rather than 2025 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government (and ultimately taxpayers) would fund the new benefit; the bill's text did not include its own funding source. Medicare Advantage plans and insurers selling standalone dental and vision coverage would face a new public benefit competing with their supplemental products.

drawbacks.text: The new benefit was phased in slowly and tightly capped: Medicare would pay only 80% of dental costs from 2025 (30% in 2023), eyeglass lenses and frames were limited to $100 each, and hearing aids were limited to one per ear every four years [S3].

The bill left financing unstated in its text — it added a broad new entitlement to Medicare without specifying how it would be paid for, and gave the Health Secretary wide discretion to add prior-authorization requirements and other limits that could narrow what patients actually receive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to seniors missing teeth, hearing, and sight would have been large and concrete — Medicare today pays for none of this outside rare hospital-linked cases, and out-of-pocket costs for dentures and hearing aids routinely run into thousands of dollars. The costs are real: new federal spending (this bill did not specify its own funding source) and a heavier administrative load on Medicare. The phase-in and caps (80% payment rates, $100 glasses limits, one hearing aid per ear per four years) kept the price down but also made the benefit less generous than supporters wanted. None of that weighing got tested, because the bill never received a single hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and their health subcommittees in July 2021, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on July 1, 2021, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees [S1, S5].
It drew 114 cosponsors, all Democrats, but no Republican support [S4].

After referral to the health subcommittees, no further action was taken; the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new benefit; the outcome preserves the status quo in which seniors pay privately or go without dental, vision, and hearing care. Insurers selling supplemental dental and vision coverage keep that market intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers selling supplemental dental and vision plans

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 114 original cosponsors [S1, S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up: no markup, no committee vote, and no report after its referral in July 2021 [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed adding new Medicare benefits during the Build Back Better negotiations; no Republican cosponsored this bill [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All 114 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the chamber's Republicans supported the bill; with a Democratic House leadership focused on the narrower Build Back Better package, the bill never advanced in committee [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Medicare Advantage insurers and Medigap insurers
industries.note: Millions of seniors buy private supplemental plans mainly to get dental, vision, and hearing coverage; a universal Medicare benefit would displace much of that market even as it brought billions in new federal health spending into the system. Sources do not document the industry's position on this specific bill.

industries.industry: Dentists, optometrists, audiologists, and hearing-aid makers
industries.note: A new Medicare benefit would route large new public payments to these providers and device makers, including 80% federal payment for hearing aids and dentures. Sources do not document their positions on the bill.
